claims.text: Adding fine, uniformly distributed Y2O3 nanoparticles to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance relative to the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3 addition will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
Powder-metallurgy processing is suitable for incorporating Y2O3 nanoparticles into refractory alloys.
Y2O3 particles provide nanoscale sinks for radiation-induced defects.
Y2O3–matrix heterointerfaces promote recombination of radiation-induced point defects.
Interfaces between Y2O3 nanoparticles and the matrix absorb radiation-induced defects.
Defect absorption and recombination at Y2O3–matrix interfaces mitigate the accumulation of defect clusters.
Reduced defect-cluster accumulation delays the onset of radiation damage.
A low volume fraction of Y2O3 nanoparticles will not adversely affect the load-bearing matrix.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will exhibit less radiation-induced swelling or a lower defect-cluster density than the unmodified baseline.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will retain yield strength better than the unmodified baseline after irradiation.
The proposed effect will hold at irradiation levels and temperatures relevant to plasma-facing fusion operation.
Outside the reactor-relevant dose or temperature range, the defect-sink mechanism may not produce a clearly observable effect.
The defect-sink mechanism of oxide dispersoids is supported in other refractory material systems.
